name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 24 October 1970

clue.text: No fiction an empty tummy to Figaro

definitions.note: Figaro is an example: the barber who sings that he is the city's handyman

blocks.note: the opposite of fiction is fact
nothing at all, the letter shaped like zero
a shortened, homely word for the stomach

explanation.surface: A hungry barber in an opera, his stomach empty and no tall tale about it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Rossini's Barber of Seville, Figaro sings 'Largo al factotum', calling himself the town's do-everything man.
explanation.definitionFit: Figaro is the classic operatic jack-of-all-trades, a servant employed to do every kind of job.

clue.text: Outside bloomer seen in the stalls?

definitions.text: Outside bloomer seen in the stalls?

blocks.clueFragment: Outside bloomer seen in the stalls?
blocks.note: surface reading: a garden flower growing outdoors, glimpsed from the theatre seats
setter's reading: cattle and sheep kept in stalls being fattened, the bulky ones with plenty outside them

explanation.surface: A flower spotted from the theatre's stalls, or blooming just outside them.
explanation.walkthrough: Stock is a garden flower, and fat is what lies on the outside; the stalls are cattle stalls, not theatre seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Livestock fattened for market are housed in byres and pens, and a stock is also a scented garden flower.

clue.text: Daggers left here too?

blocks.note: surface reading: a place where weapons are handed in
setter's reading: the phrase cloak and dagger, so if one is deposited here the other might be as well

explanation.surface: Visitors asked to hand in their weapons at the door.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke rests on the stock phrase 'cloak and dagger': where cloaks are left, why not daggers too?
explanation.definitionFit: A room in a theatre or hotel where guests deposit coats and bags for safekeeping during their visit.

clue.text: Burn to give battle

blocks.note: surface reading: set fire to something; setter's reading: a burn is a Scottish stream, the animal's home
setter's reading: the creature famous for fighting back fiercely against hunting hounds

explanation.surface: An order to set things alight before going into battle.
explanation.walkthrough: A burn is a Scottish word for a stream, not fire; the creature of the stream is renowned for fighting when cornered.
explanation.definitionFit: This aquatic mammal lives along rivers and streams and was traditionally hunted with hounds, putting up a fierce fight.

clue.text: Sue's upset about Les lie to no purpose

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for the adjective; both describe effort that achieves nothing

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so its letters end up in a new order
about means surrounding, so one set of letters goes around the other

blocks.note: the name with its possessive s, taken as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sue is upset about a lie Les told, and it all achieves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled letters of Sue's wrap around Les.
explanation.definitionFit: Something useless serves no end, having no practical benefit or worthwhile result at all.

clue.text: One king's returned to to country

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
King Lear, Shakespeare's monarch, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: A monarch comes home to his land.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled 'to' is a printing slip in the original paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a nation in the Middle East, founded as a modern state in 1948.

clue.text: A playful tussle to Hook

blocks.note: surface reading: a romp, perhaps with Captain Hook of Peter Pan
setter's reading: the rugby set piece where the hooker tries to hook the ball back with his foot

explanation.surface: A friendly wrestle with Peter Pan's pirate captain.
explanation.walkthrough: Hook is not the pirate: in rugby the hooker heels the ball out of the pack in a set piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough, confused struggle, and in rugby the old name for the scrum where forwards push for possession.

clue.text: Quaker's role of writer

blocks.note: acting as means playing the role of
the pen is the instrument that writes

explanation.surface: A member of the Society of Friends taking the part of an author.
explanation.walkthrough: Quaker is not the religious group: it is something that quakes.
explanation.definitionFit: This poplar has leaves on flattened stalks that tremble in the slightest breeze, hence the name quaking tree.

clue.text: Mercy! the fool's in the field

indicators.note: being in somewhere means placed inside it, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: a nit is a silly person
a ley is a meadow or grassland field

explanation.surface: A cry for mercy because some idiot has wandered onto the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenity is gentleness and leniency, showing clemency rather than harshness toward wrongdoers.

clue.text: Winter puts him on edge

blocks.note: surface reading: the cold season makes someone nervous
setter's reading: in cold weather on the ice this person balances on the thin edge of a blade

explanation.surface: Someone who gets jumpy when the cold months come round.
explanation.definitionFit: A person gliding on ice balances on the narrow blade's edge, a sport of frozen ponds and rinks.

clue.text: Fishy come-hither gesture in Lakeland

definitions.note: a place in Lakeland: the phrase stands for a village there

blocks.note: a freshwater fish
a beck is a beckoning nod or motion, as in 'at his beck and call'

explanation.surface: Someone making a suspicious beckoning gesture in the Lake District.
explanation.walkthrough: Lakeland is the Lake District in north-west England; there 'beck' also means a stream, fitting the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Troutbeck is a real village in the Lake District of Cumbria, near Windermere.

clue.text: See encouragement of a murderous Jack

blocks.note: first meaning: a cathedral city with its own bishop, in North Yorkshire
second meaning: urging Jack the Ripper to carry on slashing, read as two words

explanation.surface: Watch someone egg on a killer named Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: See is the noun for a bishop's diocese, not the verb; split the answer as RIP ON and it cheers on Jack the Ripper.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripon is an English cathedral city that gives its name to a diocese, and a see is a bishop's seat.

clue.text: He speculates he'll be at the receiving end

definitions.text: he'll be at the receiving end

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who takes on bets or risks, a gambler

blocks.clueFragment: he'll be at the receiving end
blocks.note: second meaning: a person who accepts or receives what is offered

explanation.surface: A gambler expects to end up on the wrong end of things.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who accepts a wager is called this, and so is anyone who receives or grabs what is given.

clue.text: Pourboire required here

blocks.note: surface reading: a French word seemingly about pouring drinks
setter's reading: the French word for a tip, left for the waiter in a small café

explanation.surface: A sign saying a gratuity is expected on the premises.
explanation.walkthrough: Pourboire, literally 'for drinking', is French for a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French café or bar where a waiter would expect a tip.

clue.text: They concern this or that

blocks.note: surface reading: vague matters about various things
setter's reading: picking one option out of two alternatives

explanation.surface: A vague remark about things that worry people.
explanation.definitionFit: Decisions between alternatives are selections, each one picking between options like this one or that one.

clue.text: Circus act to delight Mrs Partlet?

definitions.text: Circus act to delight Mrs Partlet?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a rooster jumping through a ring under the big top
Mrs Partlet is the hen, wife of Chanticleer in Chaucer, who would enjoy watching her mate perform

explanation.surface: A circus turn put on to please a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Partlet is the traditional name of a hen, from Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale; split the answer and you see the bird and the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means exultant and triumphant, crowing with joy, and literally a rooster with a ring.

clue.text: There is something logical about a boy

blocks.note: re means concerning
taken as written
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain lad has a rational streak.
explanation.definitionFit: Rational thought and sound sense, the faculty of thinking clearly and drawing sensible conclusions.

clue.text: A Charles II screen

blocks.note: surface reading: a decorative room screen in Restoration style
setter's reading: the cover of foliage that hid the king in a tree after the battle of Worcester

explanation.surface: A piece of furniture from the Restoration period.
explanation.walkthrough: After defeat at Worcester in 1651, Charles II hid in the Boscobel tree; Royal Oak Day celebrated his escape.
explanation.definitionFit: The foliage of the Royal Oak concealed the fugitive prince from Cromwell's soldiers searching below.

clue.text: Red-going but law abiding drivers

blocks.note: surface reading: motorists who drive through red lights; setter's reading: political reds
setter's reading: motorists who keep to the correct side of the road where traffic drives on that side

explanation.surface: Motorists who run red lights yet otherwise obey the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain and Australia traffic keeps to that side of the road, so obeying the law keeps you there; reds are socialists.
explanation.definitionFit: Socialists and radicals are called reds, and in this sense law-abiding motorists stay on that side of the road.

clue.text: Caps over the windmill? Frocks too!

definitions.note: a description of the thing the caps sit on; the answer is the mill body

blocks.note: first meaning: a smock mill has a rotating cap set over its sloping tower
second meaning: loose overgarments like those worn by farm labourers or artists

explanation.surface: Hats thrown over the mill, and dresses too.
explanation.walkthrough: A smock mill is a windmill whose tower looks like a countryman's smock; its cap turns the sails into the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: These loose garments are dresses or overalls, and a type of windmill bears the same name under its cap.

clue.text: Hair on and off

blocks.note: first meaning: a long tress of false hair added to a hairstyle
second meaning: the device that turns a light or machine on or off

explanation.surface: Hair that is worn sometimes and not at other times.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpiece of added tresses bears this name, and so does the control that flips power between states.

clue.text: The whispering head of Salem House

definitions.text: The whispering head of Salem House

blocks.note: surface reading: a headmaster who speaks softly
setter's reading: the school in David Copperfield, run by a cruel master who could only whisper

explanation.surface: A softly spoken headmaster in charge of a school.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield, the brutal head of Salem House has no voice and speaks in a whisper.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Creakle is the Dickens character who runs Salem House school, notorious for his whispering and his cane.

clue.text: Force; the general takes note he has about a company

indicators.note: taking something on means adding it, so one piece follows the other
about means surrounding, so these letters wrap around the others

blocks.note: the usual short form of general
a musical note
the military abbreviation for a company of soldiers

explanation.surface: A general has a note sent round his company by force.
explanation.walkthrough: Coy is the army's written abbreviation for company.
explanation.definitionFit: Cogency is persuasive power, the strength of an argument that compels people to agree.

clue.text: A village he associated with Romeo and Juliet

definitions.text: A village he associated with Romeo and Juliet

blocks.note: surface reading: a rural place linked with Shakespeare's lovers

blocks.clueFragment: he associated with Romeo and Juliet
blocks.note: setter's reading: the composer who wrote the opera A Village Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: Someone who links a country village with the star-crossed lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: A Village Romeo and Juliet is an opera by an English composer, based on a Swiss story.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick Delius composed the opera A Village Romeo and Juliet, first staged in Berlin in 1907.

clue.text: Backing me and pepping up — that's showing love

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
invigorating or refreshing, like a cold wind

explanation.surface: Someone supporting and cheering me on, a real sign of affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support, but it signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugging someone is a physical gesture of affection, holding them closely in one's arms.

clue.text: Applause for the villain

blocks.note: first meaning: a shout of approval for a performer
second meaning: a hired ruffian or assassin, an Italian word

explanation.surface: The audience cheering the baddie of the play.
explanation.definitionFit: The shout means well done, and as a noun it names a desperado or hired killer in old plays.

clue.text: Exhausted by a shopping spree?

definitions.note: describes money used up, so it fits as a past participle

blocks.note: first meaning: worn out, with no energy left
second meaning: the way money is paid out in a burst of buying

explanation.surface: Worn out after a day of buying in the shops.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means tired out, and it is also the past tense of paying money out for goods.

clue.text: For a toff, the Oceanic '

blocks.note: first meaning: a fashionable, well-dressed gentleman
second meaning: the long rolling waves of the open sea

explanation.walkthrough: The clue was cut off in the newspaper's printing; what remains gives both meanings. A toff is a British word for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: A dandy or fine gentleman was once called this, and it also names the heaving rise of ocean waves.

clue.text: Classical mountain house that is 4 in US

definitions.note: the cross-reference appears misprinted; it stands for a state of the US

blocks.note: Mount Ida, in Crete and in Troy, famous in Greek myth
the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A house on a mountain of ancient legend, somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The '4' looks like a garbled cross-reference in the printed puzzle; the sense required is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is a north-western American state, famous for potatoes and the Rocky Mountains.

clue.text: Thinks of starting a family?

blocks.note: first meaning: imagines or devises an idea
second meaning: becomes pregnant with a child

explanation.surface: Someone considering having children.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means forming an idea in the mind, and also becoming pregnant with a baby.

clue.text: Lowers the head before some front doors

definitions.note: a description of what the answer is: the platform in front of a door

blocks.note: first meaning: bends forward and down
second meaning: in North America, the small porch or set of steps at a house entrance

explanation.surface: Someone ducking their head on the way in through a low doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is American, from Dutch: a stoop is the raised step outside a front door.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means bending the body downward, and the noun names porch steps at an entrance.

clue.text: Pushers on the road of Tennyson's Cathay?

definitions.text: Pushers on the road of Tennyson's Cathay?

blocks.note: setter's reading: riders who push pedals along the highway
Tennyson wrote 'Better fifty years of Europe than a cycle of Cathay', taken here as a bicycle

explanation.surface: Drug dealers on the Silk Road in Tennyson's poetic China.
explanation.walkthrough: In Locksley Hall Tennyson meant an age of history by 'a cycle of Cathay'; the clue reads it as a bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: Riders of bicycles push pedals as they travel along roads, and Tennyson's line mentions a cycle.
